item.title: Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters
item.description:
Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else.

Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone.

  • "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute.

Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change.

  • A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut.
  • Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News.
  • If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime.

The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress.

  • Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared.
  • But progress has stalled since 2020, as rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel development and government policy reversals offset gains in clean energy.
  • "The past decade demonstrates both what climate policy can achieve and the consequences of inaction," states Climate Action Tracker's latest report, issued in Turkey.

State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities.

  • A warming world is already affecting virtually all of us, probably in ways we don't think about most of the time — whether it's wildfire smoke, higher insurance premiums or, you know, hotter weather.

Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer.

  • Homeowners in areas that face greater wildfire and wind risks generally pay higher insurance premiums, according to a Government Accountability Office report published earlier this year.

Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick:

  • An AI revolution happening faster than most of us can process, other than that it might end our jobs — or humanity.
  • A real-life spy and affair scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that seems pulled straight from Hollywood.
  • Wars and geopolitical turmoil that have sent energy prices soaring.
  • And, of course, there's affordability, which dominated this month's U.S. elections, including among victorious Democrats who didn't emphasize climate change.

Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed.

By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly.

  • Over the next two years, respondents ranked economic confrontation between countries as the biggest risk, with extreme weather, worsened by climate change, in fourth place.
  • Over the next decade, extreme weather topped the list, followed by biodiversity loss and critical changes to Earth's systems.

How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police.

  • This year's attendance is dwarfing prior years and approaching 100,000, according to United Nations and Bloomberg News data.
  • Official government negotiations are at the center, producing agreements that influence domestic policies and investments.
  • Surrounding them are increasingly crowded circles of events, from trade shows to protests, where you often capture the zeitgeist of each year's confab.

Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification.

  • Organizers launched a voluntary pledge Monday to make AI more climate-friendly, including encouraging cleaner electricity and greater transparency about data centers' environmental impacts.
  • The initiative I mentioned earlier aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 23% to 35% by 2035.

Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic.

  • In 2024, prominent climate leaders, including former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, called for a major overhaul focused more on implementing existing promises.
  • Even the UN's top climate official, Simon Stiell, acknowledged Saturday that the process needs to evolve. "Can the process be better optimized? Absolutely," he said.

Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year.

  • Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders of China and India skipped it, sending lower-level officials instead.

Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey).

Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement.

  • Many reporters, including myself, spent much of the time asking officials whether they thought newly elected President Trump would really withdraw from the deal like he promised on the campaign trail. Boy, were we naive back then.
  • In Dubai in 2023, an oil-rich country hosting a climate conference drew predictable criticism. Yet that COP produced the first global agreement calling for a transition away from fossil fuels.

The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.

item.title: Scammers are sending fake emails to people worried about Nvidia's stock
item.description:
Scammers are already exploiting the scandal surrounding Nvidia to lure unsuspecting investors and business professionals into downloading malware.

Why it matters: AI is making it easier for criminals to capitalize on the news cycle and tailor scams to specific audiences before people have time to recognize the threat.

Driving the news: KnowBe4, the cybersecurity training platform, says it's seen scammer emails using the subject line "Invitation: Nvidia Executive Partnership Discussion" that purport to offer information about Nvidia's investment strategy.

  • Inside the email, recipients see a clickable image appearing to show information about Nvidia's 2026 investment parameters. Clicking it could lead to malware being downloaded onto their devices.
  • KnowBe4 started seeing signs of the scam Wednesday, just a few days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and a day before he resigned, triggering a crisis at the chip-maker.
  • KnowBe4 CEO Bryan Palma told Axios that the campaign appears to be targeting people working in finance, transportation and government. It's unclear which group is behind the emails, he added.

The big picture: The Nvidia lure is part of a growing trend in which hackers borrow a page from the marketing industry's playbook to turn breaking news into targeted phishing campaigns.

  • Just like marketers, hackers can purchase detailed contact lists and use AI to sort potential victims by industry, profession and interests, Palma said.
  • That allows them to tailor their scams to specific audiences rather than sending the same generic email to millions of people.
  • AI is also speeding up their ability to develop and launch timely schemes, Palma said.

By the numbers: Attackers are 5.4 times faster at responding to headlines in 2026 than in 2022, according to KnowBe4 data.

  • In one case, following a major celebrity's death, scammers launched an email phishing campaign within 16 hours.
  • Nearly 88% of phishing attacks tied to breaking news or planned events impersonated a globally recognized brand, according to KnowBe4.

The bottom line: Palma recommends taking a closer look at any unexpected email that appears to reference breaking news, even if the headline seems familiar.

item.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
item.description:
Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday.

Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology.

  • Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees.

Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12, requesting they appear.

  • The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations.
  • Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed.

What they're saying: "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the three committee chairmen said in a release.

  • "We look forward to meeting with the Chairmen on December 2," Nvidia said in a statement.
  • When reached for comment Tuesday, a representative for Huang pointed to a statement the former CEO made Tuesday about returning as CEO.

What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang had stepped down as CEO over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International.

  • Huang's resignation ignited requests from Congress to investigate his relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to Nvidia's AI chips.
  • Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies.

The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have raised concerns from lawmakers about whether the government did enough to crack down on Nvidia's chips finding their way to China.

item.title: Jensen Huang says he'd be "honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
item.description:
Jensen Huang acknowledged in a statement that he'd be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO.

Why it matters: A push to reinstate Huang began almost as soon as he exited the company, but Nvidia's board said it isn't currently considering reinstating the former CEO.

What they're saying: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang's statement said.

  • "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
  • The Wall Street Journal first reported Huang's statement.

Yes, but: Nvidia's board made clear Tuesday during its earnings call that Huang is not under consideration to return as CEO, AP reports.

State of play: Multiple analyses and reports have mentioned a slew of replacement candidates for Huang's successor at Nvidia.

  • President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the role. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look for outside candidates.
  • Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is currently serving as the company's interim CEO.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang resigned as CEO after he allegedly had affairs with two Nvidia employees and former Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

  • Jensen Huang immediately faced Congressional backlash over whether Nvidia's AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether his company did enough to protect American tech.
  • He has agreed to testify before Congress next month, lawmakers said Tuesday.

Since he stepped down, Nvidia's stock has tumbled, and tech CEOs have questioned whether Jensen Huang should have been ousted in the first place.

  • His backers have included Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke.
  • Elon Musk has also backed the campaign to reinstate Jensen Huang, which has collected more than 180,000 signatures
  • Many supporters say that a lack of proof of the allegations about his relationship with Alice Huang is reason enough to reinstate him.

The other side: Nvidia's investigation into Jensen Huang's conduct is ongoing.

item.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
item.description:
Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology.

  • That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday.

Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates.

  • Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders.

What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed.

  • Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research.
  • (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.)

Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups:

  1. Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices.
  2. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder.

The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses.

  • Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said.
  • Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming large parts of the economy, which he says would limit job losses and productivity gains.

"You might interpret this as good news because it means the AI revolution is not going to destroy all the jobs or kill everybody," he said.

  • "You can also view this as very negative. Productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much. We may just continue to stagnate," he added.

The big picture: Warsh is turning to influential outsiders to challenge how the central bank thinks about the economy.

  • Affirm CEO Max Levchin told Warsh that AI has made the company's engineers five times more productive, cutting the cost of developing new features by 80%.
  • Stripe CEO Patrick Collison said new businesses launching on its platform each week have doubled from a year ago, an unprecedented surge in its 15-year history.
  • Unlike established companies, startups are more willing to let AI independently develop products and fix bugs, potentially allowing them to grow faster with fewer employees.

What to watch: Executives said AI is already delivering productivity gains in traditional industries — including sectors Andreessen said are more resistant to technological change.

  • Erik Wexler, CEO of Providence, a large nonprofit health system, said AI tools that transcribe patient appointments are saving some physicians two to four hours a day on paperwork. Wexler said that one doctor called it "life-changing."

What's next: Warsh has asked all five task forces to recommend ways to improve Fed policymaking by year-end, though he cautioned last month that some may miss the deadline.

item.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday.

Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it.

The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum.

  • Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus.
  • Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia.
  • Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector.

What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time.

  • "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts.
  • "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities.
  • "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions."

By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.)

Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion.

  • Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion.
  • The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge.

The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.

item.title: U.S. gets another D+ on premature births
item.description:
Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios

The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again, according to the latest March of Dimes report card.

Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life.

By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row.

  • It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%).

Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%.

  • Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data.
  • But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines.

Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios.

  • High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth.

What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course."

  • That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy.

What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

item.title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
item.description:
The push to reinstate former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable.

Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power.

  • Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore?
  • Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing.
  • "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergey Brin, told Bloomberg. "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable."

Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy.

  • President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Musk has also backed the effort.
  • Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke.
  • Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return.

Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset.

  • That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question.

Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips.

  • The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases and also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to the Wall Street Journal.
  • In addition to the relationships, Huang also faces questions about whether he misled Nvidia executives.

Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported Monday.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look outside the company for new leadership, while tech analyst Dan Ives has dismissed the idea of a comeback as unrealistic.

Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers.

  • In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO.
  • After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package, shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award.
  • Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable.

The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy.

  • But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward.
  • Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence.

The intrigue: The campaign to restore Huang has echoes of Sam Altman's dramatic 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, when employees, investors and powerful tech figures rallied to force a reversal.

  • OpenAI's board cited vague concerns about Altman's candor and its ability to trust him. A subsequent review found that his conduct did not mandate removal.
  • Charles Elson, corporate governance expert and founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said Altman's departure was fundamentally a dispute with his board, whereas Huang's case involves specific allegations of misconduct.
  • "What if they were to do nothing? Then you have no code of conduct," Elson said.

Altman himself acknowledged the parallels Monday, telling a Semafor conference he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," but declined to endorse Huang's return. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," he said, per Bloomberg.

The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.

item.title: United Airlines resolves "widespread system outage" that delayed flights
item.description:
United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes.

Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop.

item.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
item.description:
Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns.

Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students.

  • Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce.

Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education.

  • Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students.
  • International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates.
  • However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%.

Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios.

  • She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities.
  • "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues."
  • Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships.

By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars.

  • Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators.
  • That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported.
  • It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth.

Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing.

Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

  • International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk.
  • Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report.

Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition.

  • Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students.
  • A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices.

Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit.

  • The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue.

The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent.

  • "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect."

Go deeper: What to know about the wave of student visa cancellations

item.title: How one router may have grounded thousands of U.S. flights
item.description:
A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide.

Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel.

Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said, with thousands more delayed.

  • "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday.

Read more below.

What caused the nationwide groundstop?

What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds."

  • Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal.
  • The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris, has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide.

After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA.

  • "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement.

How did a router disrupt flights nationwide?

How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft.

  • The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft.
  • A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications.

The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds.

  • The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights.

What to know about radio frequency outages

One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions.

  • Some reports described this as a "rolling frequency outage," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time.
  • This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers.

Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy.

What happens to pilots during the outages?

Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail.

  • These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual.
  • The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage.
  • Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities.

Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected.

What does this mean for flights?

Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions.

  • Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports.
  • Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft.

What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris.

  • The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.

item.title: Average diesel prices are under $6 per gallon for the first time in months
item.description:
Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

Average U.S. diesel prices inched below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since Sept. 10 amid lower oil prices recently, per AAA data.

Why it matters: Diesel soared even more than gasoline during the Iran war, and those costs rippled throughout the economy.

  • Democrats featured high prices, especially for farmers, en route to midterm wins in typically red agricultural states.

Zoom out: The worldwide diesel supply crunch remains acute even as the broader oil market is starting to fitfully stabilize.

  • Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, damage to Middle Eastern production and shipments, throttled oil supplies, and expanded U.S. exports to meet overseas demand helped raise domestic costs.

The bottom line: Prices are now far below the Sept. 22 record of nearly $6.53 per gallon. The recent relief is real, but it's limited.

  • Average U.S. prices remain well above the prior record $5.82 per gallon set in 2022.

item.title: Employer health cost crunch is worse than projected
item.description:
There's new evidence that double-digit health cost increases were hitting employers well before the forecasts of big spikes for 2027 — forcing big changes in workplace coverage for millions of Americans.

Why it matters: The findings offer a higher-resolution view of how much health spending is putting a drag on the labor market and increasing affordability concerns for the approximately 160 million Americans who get coverage through work.

  • They also show how factors like surprise billing disputes, more cancer diagnoses and expensive specialty drugs are combining to exert cost pressure, with no immediate relief in sight.

Driving the news: A new Gallagher benefits survey of more than 3,700 firms found 36% of the companies reported premium increases of 10% or more during their most recent renewal.

  • Pharmacy costs account for a quarter or more of some companies' total health spending.
  • Cancer care is the No. 1 cost driver for about 7 in 10 firms.
  • The survey, fielded from January to March, also found employers are trying to avoid saddling workers with a disproportionate share of rising costs while struggling to balance the quality of care with their financial risk.

"The last two renewal cycles have been unlike anything we've ever seen before," said Robby White, Gallagher's U.S. benefits business line leader. "It's unsustainable, obviously. Every additional dollar that an employer spends on health care, they can't spend on their employees."

Between the lines: The 2027 coverage year was already shaping up to be painful for many employers. Projections are showing premium spikes due to rising demand for health services, more chronic disease and increased use of drugs like GLP-1s.

  • In fact, double-digit premium increases for both the 2026 and 2027 plan years suggest there are more underlying causes, according to benefits experts.
  • One leading factor is chronic disease: More people are being diagnosed with cancer at a younger age, and advanced treatments and related care can result in $10,000 a month in expenses or claims.
  • Drug costs also are surging — and not just because of demand for GLP-1s. The high cost of specialty drugs for chronic or rare conditions is prompting companies to scrutinize the way formularies are designed and how well pharmacy benefit managers administer their benefits.

White said another big cost driver is the No Surprises Act, which shielded consumers from large, unexpected medical bills but also created an expensive arbitration process.

  • The arbitration has added administrative costs and is giving providers big payouts, which add millions in costs for large employers that self-fund their health plans.
  • That's an assessment shared by big health insurers, which say the surprise billing law is creating unintended financial consequences.
  • "The [independent dispute resolution] process has now become a top-three single driver of health care cost increases for employers," Aetna president Steve Nelson told Axios, adding the company wants to work with Congress to overhaul the system.

The big picture: In a volatile health market, more employers are self-insuring and directly paying medical claims to have greater visibility and control over health costs, the Gallagher survey finds.

  • As workers get tired of high deductibles, some employers are testing copay-only plans, which vary out-of-pocket costs by medical service and steer workers to providers deemed to be providing the most value. Part of this involves more digital tools to help patients decide.
  • They're also re-evaluating their relationships with pharmacy benefit managers in response to rising drug costs, leading to what White says is a "huge shift" away from the big three PBMs — CVS Caremark, Optum Rx and Express Scripts.
  • On GLP-1s, Gallagher says the question isn't whether the drugs are effective, but whether coverage is financially sustainable. More companies are exploring direct-to-consumer sales through outside vendors and giving employees debit cards or defined subsidies.

What we're watching: Benefits experts are waiting to see how much congressionally mandated changes to PBMs' business practices bring down drug prices and improve transparency.

  • They're also watching the growing number of worker lawsuits against plan sponsors, alleging they breached their fiduciary duty by failing to negotiate reasonable prescription drug prices or keep fees reasonable.

Caitlin Owens contributed to this story.

item.title: "No sane person questions whether AI works" — but an AI bubble appears ready to pop.
item.description:
The downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang adds an explosive new risk to an already-strained AI boom, threatening to burst a financial bubble even if the technology ultimately succeeds.

Why it matters: History shows that world-changing technology and devastating financial bubbles often go hand in hand. A market reckoning won't stop the AI revolution. But as with the dot-com crash, it could vaporize trillions in investor wealth as expectations come crashing back to earth.

The big picture: "No sane person questions whether AI works. And that 'working' status is precisely what makes a bubble possible," veteran technology investor Paul Kedrosky told Axios.

  • The risks have grown as technology companies commit trillions to infrastructure, increasingly relying on debt, investments in one another and complicated financing arrangements to keep the expansion going.

Driving the news: Huang's stunning resignation Thursday has shaken confidence in the company at the center of the AI boom — and raised fresh questions about the sustainability of the broader investment frenzy.

  • Nvidia, which named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, faces a leadership vacuum at a time when the industry is already grappling with financial and political uncertainty.
  • Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has helped finance the massive expansion of computing infrastructure by investing in its customers and providing financial backstops for major projects.
  • A more cautious approach by Huang's successor could undermine confidence in projects that have depended on Nvidia's financial support.

What they're saying: RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas told Axios that Huang's departure could trigger a "wholesale bursting" of the AI bubble.

  • "The turmoil around Jensen Huang matters for the buildout if it makes lenders less confident that Nvidia will back the next round of projects," Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh told Axios.

Zoom out: The financial and political vulnerabilities were piling up well before the Nvidia scandal.

  • Spending is outpacing expected returns. AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, while Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over the same period, according to Axios reporting.
  • Valuation expectations are being reset. Anthropic's newly announced IPO terms imply a valuation well below earlier hopes of as much as $2 trillion. OpenAI also reportedly secured less cash and a lower valuation than it had hoped in a recent funding round.
  • Investors are growing more cautious. Retail traders, who have routinely bought previous AI-related market dips, instead became net sellers of U.S. stocks during the sharp Nov. 5 sell-off, according to Vanda Research.
  • Financing is getting harder. The debt-fueled expansion was already showing signs of strain before the latest turmoil. Rising borrowing costs and an avalanche of new bond offerings have made lenders wary.
  • Political opposition is growing. A wave of election victories for AI-skeptical candidates, along with widespread voter support for data center restrictions, threatens to delay construction, increase costs and undermine the assumptions behind some projects.
  • Regulatory risks are mounting. Huang's downfall has intensified bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, which increasingly appear likely to pass.

The risk: A retreat in AI investment could become self-reinforcing, turning a market correction into a much broader financial reckoning.

  • Falling valuations and tighter credit could make it harder for startups and cloud providers to finance additional data centers, reducing demand for chips, power and other infrastructure.
  • That could put further pressure on the investors, lenders and companies financing the expansion, spreading the consequences well beyond the companies developing AI models.

Yes, but: There is considerable evidence that AI itself is a real and potentially transformative technology — and that demand is growing rapidly.

  • Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up from $71 billion a month earlier.
  • OpenAI grew quarterly revenue roughly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to the Wall Street Journal, even as its adjusted operating losses reached $10.9 billion.
  • Businesses are already using AI to write software, automate tasks and perform work that previously required significant human effort.
  • Tighter U.S. export controls could also benefit American AI developers by limiting Chinese rivals' access to advanced computing power, even as they complicate Nvidia's business prospects.

The historical lesson: Some of the greatest technological transformations have been accompanied by speculative investment booms that ended painfully for investors.

  • "I have no doubt that AI will be transformative. That does not preclude a financial bubble," MIT economics professor Ricardo Caballero told Axios.
  • Caballero argues that excessive optimism may even be necessary to marshal the enormous investments required for a new technology to reach its potential.
  • Such booms can leave behind valuable infrastructure and lasting economic gains, as they did in the dot-com boom-bust cycle, even if many investors suffer losses along the way.

The bottom line: "AI can deliver enormous value to users while the companies building the infrastructure earn far less than their investors expected," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

  • Nvidia, which named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, faces a leadership vacuum at a time when the industry is already grappling with financial and political uncertainty.
  • Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has helped finance the massive expansion of computing infrastructure by investing in its customers and providing financial backstops for major projects.
  • A more cautious approach by Huang's successor could undermine confidence in projects that have depended on Nvidia's financial support.

What they're saying: RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas told Axios that Huang's departure could trigger a "wholesale bursting" of the AI bubble.

  • "The turmoil around Jensen Huang matters for the buildout if it makes lenders less confident that Nvidia will back the next round of projects," Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh told Axios.

Zoom out: The financial and political vulnerabilities were piling up well before the Nvidia scandal.

  • Spending is outpacing expected returns. AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, while Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over the same period, according to Axios reporting.
  • Valuation expectations are being reset. Anthropic's newly announced IPO terms imply a valuation well below earlier hopes of as much as $2 trillion. OpenAI also reportedly secured less cash and a lower valuation than it had hoped in a recent funding round.
  • Investors are growing more cautious. Retail traders, who have routinely bought previous AI-related market dips, instead became net sellers of U.S. stocks during the sharp Nov. 5 sell-off, according to Vanda Research.
  • Financing is getting harder. The debt-fueled expansion was already showing signs of strain before the latest turmoil. Rising borrowing costs and an avalanche of new bond offerings have made lenders wary.
  • Political opposition is growing. A wave of election victories for AI-skeptical candidates, along with widespread voter support for data center restrictions, threatens to delay construction, increase costs and undermine the assumptions behind some projects.
  • Regulatory risks are mounting. Huang's downfall has intensified bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, which increasingly appear likely to pass.

  • That could put further pressure on the investors, lenders and companies financing the expansion, spreading the consequences well beyond the companies developing AI models.

  • Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up from $71 billion a month earlier.
  • OpenAI grew quarterly revenue roughly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to the Wall Street Journal, even as its adjusted operating losses reached $10.9 billion.

  • Tighter U.S. export controls could also benefit American AI developers by limiting Chinese rivals' access to advanced computing power, even as they complicate Nvidia's business prospects.

The historical lesson: Some of the greatest technological transformations have been accompanied by speculative investment booms that ended painfully for investors.

  • "I have no doubt that AI will be transformative. That does not preclude a financial bubble," MIT economics professor Ricardo Caballero told Axios.
  • Caballero argues that excessive optimism may even be necessary to marshal the enormous investments required for a new technology to reach its potential.
  • Such booms can leave behind valuable infrastructure and lasting economic gains, as they did in the dot-com boom-bust cycle, even if many investors suffer losses along the way.

The bottom line: "AI can deliver enormous value to users while the companies building the infrastructure earn far less than their investors expected," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

item.title: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.

Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.

  • The Treasury secretary casting doubt on the quality of its financial results and leadership could be a blow to an already shaky market.
  • Since the scandal broke open in late October, Nvidia shares have shed more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization, with impacts on millions of Americans.

Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.

  • "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said.
  • "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel."

Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."

  • "This makes me think that as the board conducts the search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company," he said.

For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.

The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.

  • In recent days, Bessent has also made clear that the Commerce Department has questions to answer about why it didn't impose tighter controls on Nvidia's exports.
  • As Axios reported earlier this week, administration officials have accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of stalling curbs on Nvidia's exports.

What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

item.title: How Nvidia's scandal knocked thousands off your 401(k)
item.description:
Nvidia's near-30% stock plunge in the last month is a drag on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, many who may not realize just how much their investments are tied to the scandal-engulfed chip giant.

Why it matters: Nvidia's enormous weight in popular index funds means even those who have never purchased a single share of the company could feel the pain of its corporate upheaval in their 401(k)s.

  • The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang after he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy may have cost an average Baby Boomer thousands of dollars, according to an Axios analysis of outside estimates.

By the numbers: Index funds held nearly half of the assets in large private-sector 401(k) plans in 2023, according to the Investment Company Institute.

  • Those funds include investments tracking the S&P 500, and Nvidia accounts for roughly 8% of that index, according to Tom Graff, chief investment officer at financial planning firm Facet.
  • That exposure rises to around 14% in growth-style index funds and can reach 25% to 30% in some technology and semiconductor funds commonly found in retirement plans, Graff said.

Zoom in: For an investor with $100,000 in an S&P 500 fund, a 30% drop in Nvidia shares would knock about $2,400 off the value of that investment given an 8% S&P holding, assuming other stocks in the fund stayed flat.

  • For a growth-style tech fund with 25% exposure to Nvidia, that decline would amount to $7,500 in lost value.
  • An average Baby Boomer holds about $260,000 in their 401(k), according to Fidelity. A tech-style exposure applied to that amount of holdings would equate to about a $20,000 reduction.

Yes, but: Remember, a drop in your investment's value doesn't mean you've actually lost that cash — unless you sell your holdings.

Zoom out: The potential fallout extends beyond Nvidia itself.

  • About 40% of the S&P 500 is tied to the AI buildout, for which Nvidia is central, providing much of the financing and infrastructure needed to fuel the tech boom.
  • If Nvidia's troubles slow the pace of AI data center investment, the damage could spread to other stocks held in Americans' retirement portfolios, analyst Bob Iaccino notes to Axios via message.
  • "A lot of people are starting to realize just how much Nvidia exposure they have in funds they thought were diversified," Graff told Axios. "You don't want too much of your retirement riding on whether Nvidia has a successful transition to new leadership or not," he added.

Reality check: While Nvidia has come to define the AI trade, its competitors have also emerged as potential beneficiaries of the stock's decline.

  • "The mindset has flipped very quickly to 'who might benefit from this?'" Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers told Axios.
  • Chip-company AMD's stock went on a run, rising by more than 30% in a five-day stretch last week, contributing to a broader run in the semiconductor sector. Nvidia makes up a sizable portion of many semiconductor indices and ETFs, showing how rotation can keep bull runs alive even as single stocks falter.
  • Hyperscalers with their own chip ambitions, which at times have looked competitive with Nvidia, have also beaten the growth of the S&P 500 index over the last five days.

Reality check: For those who are direct shareholders, the widely held financial advice would always tell you not to lock in losses as a stock drops.

  • It's very unclear what the investigation will unveil.
  • Nvidia is set to report earnings on Tuesday, giving shareholders more insight into its latest quarterly performance.

The bottom line: Americans don't need to own Nvidia shares directly to have their retirement savings tied to the company's successes, or failures.

item.title: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
item.description:
Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze.

  • That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report.

Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems.

Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government.

  • If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers' worries.
  • If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts.
  • Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris.
  • Space data centers are solar-powered, but the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions.

What they're saying: Columbia University's David Sandalow, the report's lead author, told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about space data center impacts.

  • "If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care," Sandalow said. "Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks."

By the numbers: Despite those concerns, investors and tech innovators are all in on space data centers.

  • In 2025, around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers, per market research firm Quilty Space. That figure has swelled to $1.11 billion so far this year.
  • SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites, according to the Secure World Foundation.
  • Starcloud and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively.

Yes, but: Caleb Henry, Quilty Space's director of research, said that companies may be filing for more satellites than they will likely field. "They don't want to have to bump the number higher up later on," he said in an interview.

  • "We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real," Henry said, "and we just don't know that yet."

The bottom line: Researchers warned that governments and companies need to wait until space data center "risks and impacts are better understood and well managed" before putting them in orbit.

item.title: FAA back at "full operations" after Friday outage, Transportation Sec. says
item.description:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that all FAA systems are back to "full operations" after an hours-long outage Friday evening that grounded all air traffic across the U.S.

The big picture: Duffy reiterated his plea to Congress to fund upgrades to the nation's air traffic control equipment, explaining that proper upgrades could have prevented the ground stop.

Driving the news: Duffy explained that the outage was caused when a contractor performed routine maintenance on a telecommunications line to upgrade a copper wire to fiber-optic cable and install a new router.

  • "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down. So we had to switch it over from old copper," Duffy said.
  • Duffy said it's unclear whether the outage occurred because of contractor error or faulty equipment, but they are working to figure that out.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford warned that up to 5,000 flight cancellations will remain throughout today, but airlines have assured the agency that they should return to normal operations by the end of the day Sunday.

  • "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," Bedford said.
  • According to numbers from FlightAware, over 4,700 international and domestic flights have been canceled, and over 13,500 delayed, as of 11:50 am ET.

Zoom out: Bedford and Duffy both said the ground stop was ordered out of an abundance of caution for the safety of passengers and airplane crews.

  • Bedford added that they have no reason to believe a cyberattack or an AI issue prompted the outage.
  • "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious," Bedford said.

Zoom in: Duffy used the press conference to again plead with Congress to fund upgrades for the aging air traffic control system.

  • Duffy has previously said the FAA needs $30 billion to update airports and air traffic control. Congress had previously awarded $12.5 billion in July 2025 for upgrades into 2030.
  • After Friday's outage, Duffy upped the funding request to $50 billion.
  • "For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it, and the president is pushing it, but we don't get the resources," Duffy said. "And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait, America and Congress? And I think this is a sign for them to lean in. This is bipartisan."

Bedford offered a blunt assessment when reporters asked about the system's function, saying it's the "worst-kept secret in government" that it needs an upgrade.

  • "We have to keep the existing system operating at the very best of our ability," with the funding they have, he said.
  • "But," Bedford continued, "let's not kid ourselves. It will continue to break until we replace it."

item.title: AI's four colliding crises
item.description:
AI's titans were handed an extraordinary mandate: Police yourselves.

  • But the industry faces a four-pronged crisis of trust as Democrats surge to power and many Americans rebel over AI and data centers. Guardrails for the industry will be a priority for the new Congress, with some populist Republicans eager to pile on.

Why it matters: The collision of safety scares, political blows, financial turmoil and leadership scandals threatens to derail AI's once seemingly unstoppable ascent.

The big picture: Just six weeks ago, President Trump announced that top AI CEOs had agreed to a voluntary safety accord.

  • But cracks were already showing and, since then, four crises have converged.

🏛️ 1. The political crisis: AI was on the ballot for the first time during the midterm elections through a series of data center measures across America. People voted against data centers in 40 out of 41 cases, and swing-state incumbents linked to the facilities, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), were voted out.

  • Now Democrats are planning a flood of AI bills once they take control of Congress in January, Reuters reports. They'll also bring some of the most powerful AI executives to D.C. to testify.

🦺 2. The safety crisis: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach, revealed in July, was a terrifying look at what could happen if machines operate beyond humans' control — and it was the first in a wave of revelations through the summer and fall.

  • AI CEOs and engineers came forward with stark warnings about the dangers of the tech they've been building, including its potential to destroy humanity.
  • Axios' Madison Mills reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents and that unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts.

💰 3. The financial crisis: The AI trade is looking more vulnerable as investors question when or whether the industry's sky-high spending will deliver sky-high returns.

  • Tech stocks tumbled, with Nvidia falling 13% this week amid the ouster of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The stock has lost nearly 25% of its value since the first New York Times report in late October about Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy.
  • Anthropic's IPO may not be what some hoped, with its projected valuation coming in roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago.

🧐 4. The leadership crisis: Huang's stunning resignation, following revelations about affairs, is raising new questions about the vulnerability of the people running America's most powerful companies.

  • Nvidia's stock slide exemplifies the risk of putting so much power in the hands of so few AI executives.
  • Pop culture has turned on the AI titans, with three year-end films — "The Social Reckoning" and "Musk," out last month, and "Artificial," opening Christmas Day — savaging Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Reality check: The AI industry's hurdles are partly growing pains — investors start demanding returns, lawmakers seek accountability, the public grows skeptical.

  • The trust collapse echoes the moment social media companies went from Silicon Valley darlings to public enemies. But AI's reckoning — just like its rise — has come much faster.

item.title: Wholesale food prices are on the rise
item.description:
Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves.

Why it matters: Americans are already paying more for groceries. New inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up.

  • Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month.
  • These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers.
  • Wholesale food prices overall are up 1.7% from a year earlier, ending a three-month streak of annual price declines.

Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California.

  • The Iran war, meanwhile, has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food.
  • A regional grocery chain recently told Federal Reserve officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices.
  • Truck freight costs are up almost 25% over the past year, the largest annual increase since 2022 and on par with the surge seen during the pandemic-era inflation shock.

The big picture: It's unclear how much of the surge in producer prices will be passed along to consumers. But steeper price increases were already showing up at supermarket checkout counters last month.

  • Grocery prices rose 0.4%, the biggest monthly increase in 6 months, driven by higher prices for meat, dairy products and snack foods.
  • Fresh vegetable prices climbed 2%, including a nearly 8% jump in lettuce prices.

item.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status
item.description:
An international health organization has determined that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple news reports.

Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year.

  • Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts.

The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years.

  • The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break.
  • The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates remain relatively high, public health officials say they have to remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity.

Driving the news: An expert panel convened by the Pan American Health Organization made the widely expected decision following a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C.

What they're saying: "It is no surprise that the resurgence of measles has coincided with an administration that has inflicted significant damage to our health care system while spreading false claims about vaccines," said Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control.

  • "It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026," the Infectious Diseases Society said in comments prior to the decision.
  • The group cited the potential long-term toll on infants infected this year, some of whom could develop serious neurologic disease years after the initial infection.

By the numbers: There have been 5,412 confirmed cases so far this year, compared to 2,289 for all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest tally.

  • The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases.
  • Pennsylvania is in the grip of an outbreak that has accounted for more than 1,500 cases so far and six measles-associated deaths.
  • Those reports are widely considered to be an undercount, due to the lack of widespread testing and unreported instances of mild illness.

While most measles cases aren't severe, they can have long-lasting effects because of the way the virus can suppress the body's immune responses, leaving people more susceptible to other infections.

  • About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized, per the CDC.

How it works: Experts rely on disease tracking by local health departments and genetic sequencing, and can also factor vaccination rates and surveillance efforts.

  • Canada and the United Kingdom have both lost their measles elimination status over the past year.
  • The determinations are largely symbolic, but mean the virus has become endemic and is spreading freely in pockets of unvaccinated people, according to Yale epidemiologist Katelyn Jetelina.
  • Since early 2025, there have been large-scale outbreaks in West Texas, along the Utah-Arizona border and in South Carolina.

item.title: 3,000 flights cancelled as FAA ground stop chaos stretches into 2nd day
item.description:
The chaos from the FAA's nationwide ground stop lingered into early Saturday morning, with thousands of flights cancelled as airlines played catch-up.

Why it matters: Millions of travelers will find themselves inconvenienced over what the government says was simply old technology that couldn't keep up with modern upgrades.

Driving the news: As of 5:15 a.m. ET Saturday, nearly 3,300 flights into, out of, or within the United States were already cancelled for the day, per FlightAware.

  • Nearly 1,000 flights already had delays.

Between the lines: The most heavily impacted airports were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson, New York's JFK and Boston Logan.

  • Among the major airlines, FlightAware's data showed Delta more affected than United or American.

Zoom in: The ground stop wreaked havoc on college football in particular, with many schools unable to travel to their game locations.

  • ESPN reported a number of high-profile match-ups were postponed to either late Saturday or Sunday as a result.

What to watch: Whether Congress responds to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's request for $50 billion in emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
item.description:
The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January.

Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that officials in many states warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage.

  • A federal court last month struck down a portion of the rules that required chronically ill Medicaid recipients to prove their condition significantly impairs the ability to work in order to qualify for an exemption.

Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said Friday there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience."

  • Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times.
  • The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that a chaotic rollout of the requirements will disenroll more people because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements.

What they're saying: "States have made real progress, and they've been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term," said Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman.

How it works: The first-ever work rules mean Medicaid enrollees must report at least 80 hours a month of work, school or volunteering or get an exemption.

  • States were facing tight timetables for setting up systems to notify millions of recipients about the requirements — and to track whether they're complying.
  • Nebraska's early rollout of the work requirements in May led to confusion and coverage denials due to unsubmitted paperwork, per KFF Health News.

What we're watching: Democrats who will control Congress next year intend to push for more delays, or to scrap the work requirements altogether.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with more details on the delay.
